narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence; being in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly the middle of the class among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 18 was the second most important factor. This score is far below the average of 37 among accepted applicants and therefore also pulled the outcome heavily toward not passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.20 worked mildly in the opposite direction, slightly increasing the chance of success because it sits close to the typical GPA of students who were admitted.

Taken together, the model saw your low year-three ranking and very low LSAT performance as clear signals that the bar exam would be a significant challenge, outweighing the small positive signal from your GPA.

What you should do next is focus on improving the areas the model flagged. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, while also strengthening your study habits so that your class rank improves in future years. With clearer evidence of stronger academic performance, your next application will be viewed much more favorably. (218 words)
